title: Kimchi Jjigae
subtitle: kimchi and pork stew
excerpt: Kimchi jjigae is a bold, sour Korean stew made from well-fermented kimchi, pork belly, and tofu simmered in a spicy broth. It uses older, more acidic kimchi that is past its best for eating raw. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Kimchi jjigae is one of the most popular Korean stews. It is a practical dish that makes use of kimchi that has fermented long enough to become very sour.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the tofu for up to 2 months. Add fresh tofu when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch easily. The stew keeps well in the fridge for 3 days and improves overnight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make a day ahead for deeper flavour.

Heat the oil in a dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the pork belly pieces and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, turning, until lightly browned on all sides.
Add the garlic and onion and cook for 2 minutes. Add a large amount of well-fermented kimchi (about 300 g, roughly chopped) and stir to combine. Cook for 3 minutes until the kimchi is heated through.
Add the gochujang, chilli flakes, and soy sauce. Stir to coat everything in the paste. Pour in the water and bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes. The pork should be tender and the broth a deep red colour.
Add the tofu and simmer for a further 5 minutes. Add the spring onion and drizzle sesame oil over the top. Serve straight from the pot with steamed rice.

attrs.fix: Use older, more fermented kimchi. Fresh kimchi will not give the same sourness. You can also add 1 tablespoon of rice vinegar to sharpen the flavour.
The pieces need more time. Simmer for a further 10 minutes with the lid on. Pork belly is fatty and becomes tender with longer cooking.
Simmer with the lid off for the last 10 minutes to reduce and concentrate the flavour.

content.text: Kimchi jjigae is the kind of dish Korean home cooks make without a recipe. It is on the table in the coldest months and eaten year-round. The stew is served straight from the pot. Each person eats it alongside a bowl of rice. Leftover stew tastes even better the next day.
